q: After a federal jury convicts a defendant of robbing a pharmacy, a juror's affidavit reports three things. First, during deliberations another juror announced that she had driven from the defendant's apartment to the pharmacy the night before and that the trip took twelve minutes, not the forty minutes the alibi required. Second, two jurors drank beer at lunch on the last day and seemed drowsy that afternoon. Third, the foreperson said that he had once been robbed and that "people like this always lie about timing." The defendant moves for a new trial. Which matter may the court consider in deciding the motion?
o: The juror's report of her own timed drive, which brought facts into the jury room that were never admitted at trial.
The jurors' lunchtime drinking, because the beer was bought outside the courthouse and was not part of the jury process.
The foreperson's account of his own robbery, because a juror's experiences before trial are not part of deliberations.
None of the three, because each matter was described or discussed only while the jury was deliberating in private.
oe: Correct. Her drive created new evidence outside the trial record and brought it into deliberations. That is extraneous prejudicial information under 606(b)(2)(A), and a juror may testify that it happened.
Tanner treats juror intoxication as internal, whatever the source of the alcohol. What matters is the nature of the allegation, not where the substance came from.
Jurors' life experiences are internal by nature (Warger). The foreperson's remark is not outside information about this case.
Too broad. 606(b) has exceptions for extraneous information, outside influence, and verdict-form errors, and the timed drive fits the first one.

q: During a long federal fraud trial, the lone holdout juror asks the court security officer whether the jury can go home. The officer replies, "The judge wants a verdict by Friday, or you'll all be stuck here for weeks." The jury convicts on Thursday. The holdout's affidavit describes the officer's remark and states that it was the reason she changed her vote. On the defendant's motion for a new trial, what may the court receive from the juror?
o: Her account of what the officer said, but not her account of how the remark affected her decision to change her vote.
Both the remark and its effect on her vote, because the remark falls within an exception that allows the juror to testify.
Neither the remark nor its effect, because pressure to reach a verdict is an internal feature of every jury's deliberations.
The remark only if the officer confirms it, because a juror cannot testify about events that occurred during deliberations.
oe: Correct. A remark from court personnel is an outside influence (606(b)(2)(B)). Even within an exception, jurors may not testify about the effect on their own thought processes. The court decides prejudice objectively.
An exception permits testimony that the influence occurred. It never opens up a juror's mental processes.
Pressure the jurors put on each other is internal, but this pressure came from a court officer outside the jury, which makes it an outside influence.
The exception allows the juror's own testimony. Confirmation from the officer is not required.

q: After a federal jury convicts a Latino defendant of assault, a juror's affidavit states that during deliberations another juror said the defendant "did it because he's Mexican, and Mexican men take whatever they want," and that two others laughed and agreed. The affidavit also states that a third juror said, "I just didn't believe a word he said on the stand." The defendant moves for a new trial. How should the court approach the affidavit?
o: Consider the ethnic remark and decide whether racial animus was a significant motivating factor, but disregard the credibility remark.
Consider both remarks, because a juror's credibility judgment about a minority defendant falls within the same constitutional exception.
Consider neither remark, because both were made during deliberations and no juror received information from outside the room.
Grant a new trial without further inquiry, because any racial remark during deliberations violates the defendant's jury right.
oe: Correct. Peña-Rodriguez allows the inquiry when a juror's statement shows reliance on racial stereotypes or animus. The court must then decide whether it was a significant motivating factor. A bare credibility judgment stays protected.
Nothing in the credibility remark shows racial bias. The Peña exception is limited to clear statements of racial animus.
Peña recognizes a constitutional exception to 606(b) for racial bias, even though the remark is otherwise internal.
No new trial is automatic. The statement must tend to show that animus was a significant motivating factor, and offhand comments may not meet that threshold.

q: Variation: The same ethnic remark is made during deliberations in a federal civil employment-discrimination suit brought by a Latino plaintiff, which the jury resolves for the employer. The plaintiff relies on Peña-Rodriguez in moving for a new trial. Which statement most accurately describes the plaintiff's position?
o: Peña rested on the criminal defendant's Sixth Amendment jury right, so whether a parallel exception reaches civil verdicts is unsettled.
Peña expressly applies to civil and criminal verdicts alike, so the court must inquire whether animus motivated the verdict.
The remark is extraneous prejudicial information about a party, so 606(b)(2)(A) permits the inquiry without any constitutional claim.
Racial bias can never be used to impeach a civil verdict, because Rule 606(b) treats civil verdicts as final once entered.
oe: Correct. Problem I.1 raises exactly this question. A civil litigant has to rely on due process or Seventh Amendment arguments, and the law is debated.
Peña's holding is grounded in the Sixth Amendment, which applies only in criminal cases. It did not decide civil cases.
A juror's own prejudice is internal, not extraneous. The rule-based exceptions do not reach it.
That overstates the law. Whether a civil exception exists is an open question, not a settled no.
topic: Jury secrecy — Peña in civil cases
pre: After a federal jury convicts a Latino defendant of assault, a juror's affidavit states that during deliberations another juror said the defendant "did it because he's Mexican, and Mexican men take whatever they want," and that two others laughed and agreed. The affidavit also states that a third juror said, "I just didn't believe a word he said on the stand." The defendant moves for a new trial. How should the court approach the affidavit?

q: In a federal wrongful-death trial arising from a highway crash, the jury returns a verdict form awarding $50,000. Two days later a juror tells counsel that (1) every juror had agreed to $500,000, but the foreperson left off a zero when filling in the form, and (2) the foreperson told the jury that her own son had died in a similar crash, although she had said in voir dire that nothing in her past would affect her. The plaintiff seeks relief based on both disclosures. What may the juror's testimony be used to establish?
o: The error in writing the agreed amount on the form, but not the foreperson's statements about her son's death.
Both disclosures, because recording errors and dishonest voir dire answers are each recognized exceptions to the rule.
The foreperson's statements, because concealing a fact during voir dire happens before deliberations and is not covered by the rule.
Neither disclosure, because the juror learned of both matters only by taking part in the jury's private deliberations.
oe: Correct. 606(b)(2)(C) permits testimony that a mistake was made in entering the verdict on the form. Warger holds that deliberation statements cannot be used to show dishonesty in voir dire.
Voir dire dishonesty is not an exception. Warger rejected that route.
The proof would come from what she said during deliberations, and Warger says that testimony is barred even if offered to show voir dire dishonesty.
The verdict-form exception exists precisely so that clerical errors in recording the actual verdict can be corrected.

q: A state homicide statute requires that the defendant act "purposely or knowingly," and a separate statute provides that voluntary intoxication "may not be taken into consideration in determining the existence of a mental state." The defendant was found in a crashed car beside two victims with a blood-alcohol level of .30. The State offers his slurred statements to the first officer, "I shot them, I shot them," as admissions. The defense offers his blood-alcohol evidence. For which purpose is the evidence most clearly relevant?
o: To suggest that his slurred statements to the first officer were unreliable and deserve little weight as admissions.
To suggest that a person that drunk was unlikely to have acted with the purpose that the homicide statute requires.
To suggest that he could not have known the handgun was loaded at the moment it discharged inside the car.
To suggest under Rule 403 that the State's intent evidence is outweighed by the confusion that intoxication creates.
oe: Correct. The statute makes intoxication immaterial only to mental state. The reliability of the State's admissions is a different fact of consequence, so the evidence is probative and material for that purpose.
This is the exact use the statute forbids. Under Egelhoff, substantive law can make intoxication immaterial to mental state.
Knowledge is a mental state, so the statute removes intoxication from that question too.
Rule 403 is a ground to exclude evidence, not a way to make immaterial evidence relevant. Materiality comes from the substantive law.

q: A payroll manager is charged with embezzlement. To prove motive, the prosecution offers an email announcing a surprise audit that would have exposed the missing funds. The email was sent to a shared departmental inbox that twelve people could read. No evidence yet shows that the manager opened it, but the prosecutor says a later witness will testify that the manager attended a meeting where the audit was discussed. The defense objects that the email is irrelevant. How should the court proceed?
o: Admit the email on condition that evidence will be introduced sufficient for a jury to find that the manager knew of the audit.
Exclude the email until the judge personally finds by a preponderance of the evidence that the manager actually read it.
Admit the email without condition, because an impending audit gives every employee with access to the funds a reason to steal.
Exclude the email unless the prosecution first proves beyond a reasonable doubt that the manager knew about the audit.
oe: Correct. The audit shows motive only if the manager knew of it. That is conditional relevance under 104(b): the court needs evidence from which a jury could reasonably find knowledge, and it may admit subject to later proof (Cox), striking the email if the proof never comes.
Knowledge here is a 104(b) question for the jury, decided on a sufficiency standard. It is not a 104(a) finding for the judge.
An audit the manager didn't know about could not have motivated him. That missing link is the reason 104(b) exists.
Preliminary facts are never held to the criminal standard of proof. The test is jury sufficiency by a preponderance.

q: A police officer charged with manslaughter claims self-defense. He shot a man who stepped out of a nightclub doorway holding a guitar case. He offers a department bulletin issued two weeks earlier warning that local gang members had been hiding sawed-off shotguns in instrument cases. The case turned out to contain only a guitar. For the bulletin to be relevant to his defense, what additional fact must the evidence support?
o: That the officer had read the bulletin or been briefed on it before he fired, so that it could have shaped his fear.
That the man who was shot was in fact a member of one of the gangs described in the bulletin's warning to officers.
That the bulletin's warning was accurate and that gang members had actually been hiding weapons in instrument cases.
That the guitar case was large enough to hold a sawed-off shotgun of the type described in the bulletin's warning.
oe: Correct. Self-defense turns on what the officer reasonably believed. A bulletin he never saw could not have affected his belief, so his knowledge is a 104(b) condition (Violin Case, Problem 1.6).
The officer's reasonable belief matters, not the man's actual affiliation. The officer didn't know the man's gang status.
Even an inaccurate warning could make his fear reasonable if he relied on it. What matters is that he knew of it, not whether it was true.
This might affect the weight of the evidence, but the essential link is whether the officer knew of the bulletin.

q: A woman charged with killing her boyfriend claims self-defense. She testifies that months earlier he told her he had once broken a man's jaw with a tire iron, and that this was why she feared for her life when he reached for the toolbox. In closing, the prosecutor will argue that she made up the story. The defense offers a certified record of the boyfriend's conviction for assaulting a man with a tire iron. She never saw the record. What is the strongest basis for admitting it?
o: To corroborate her testimony that he told her about the beating, which makes her claim of genuine fear more believable.
To prove his violent character as evidence that he attacked first, which Rule 405(b) permits in self-defense cases.
To prove her state of mind directly, because the conviction reflects what a reasonable person in her position would have known.
To impeach the boyfriend's credibility under Rule 609, because the assault was punishable by more than one year.
oe: Correct. Under the en banc James decision, records the defendant never saw can still corroborate her account of what she was told. That bolsters the credibility of her testimony about her state of mind.
Character is not an essential element of self-defense. Rule 405 limits a victim's violent character to reputation or opinion.
She didn't know of the record, so it can't show her state of mind directly. Its value is as corroboration.
The boyfriend is dead and not a witness. Rule 609 impeaches only a witness's testimony.

q: An engineer is charged with unlawfully keeping a competitor's stolen design files on encrypted drives found in a fireproof safe in the bedroom closet he shares with his husband. He claims his husband alone used the safe. The government offers evidence that the safe also held the engineer's passport, his prescription medication, and his birth certificate. The defense objects that these lawful personal items prove nothing about the charged crime. How should the court rule?
o: Overrule the objection, because the items tend to show he personally used the safe and so knew of and controlled its contents.
Sustain the objection, because possessing a passport and medication is lawful and cannot prove an element of the charged offense.
Sustain the objection unless the government first shows that the engineer placed the drives in the safe himself.
Overrule the objection, because once evidence is found at the scene of a crime, Rule 402 makes it admissible for any purpose.
oe: Correct. The chain of inference runs from personal documents, to personal use of the safe, to knowledge and control of the drives. The evidence need not be conclusive: a brick is not a wall (Passports, Problem 1.2).
Lawful items can still be circumstantial evidence of disputed facts such as control and knowledge.
Rule 401 asks only whether the evidence makes a fact more or less probable. It does not require proof of the ultimate fact first.
Rule 402 admits relevant evidence. Where the evidence was found doesn't establish relevance, and other rules can still exclude it.

q: A defendant is tried for being a felon in possession of a firearm. His qualifying felony is a seven-year-old armed-robbery conviction. Before trial he offers to stipulate that he has a prior felony conviction, and he tells the court that he intends to testify. The government wants to tell the jury that the prior felony was armed robbery, both to prove his status and to impeach him when he testifies. How should the court rule?
o: Accept the stipulation for the status element, but allow the robbery to be named for impeachment if the Rule 609 test is met.
Allow the government to name the robbery for both purposes, because a prosecutor may always choose its own proof of an element.
Bar any mention of the robbery for any purpose, because the defendant's stipulation removed the conviction from the case.
Allow the name only for status, because Rule 609 lets jurors learn of a prior felony but never the name of the crime.
oe: Correct. Under Old Chief, refusing a stipulation to status in favor of naming the offense is an abuse of discretion. Impeachment is a separate question under 609(a)(1)(B), and Estrada's practice of naming the crime may apply there, with a limiting instruction.
Old Chief makes an exception to that general principle for status elements when the defense offers a stipulation.
A stipulation to status doesn't affect impeachment. If the defendant testifies, Rule 609 controls that separate use.
This gets both uses backward. Old Chief bars the name for status, while 609 practice generally allows it for impeachment.

q: At a murder trial, the defense concedes that the victim died of stab wounds but disputes premeditation. The prosecution offers four items. Which is most likely to be excluded under Rule 403?
o: Photographs of the body after three weeks outdoors, showing decomposition and damage by animals that the medical examiner did not rely on.
A photograph of fourteen wounds, including defensive cuts, which the medical examiner will use to explain why the wounds show deliberation.
A diagram prepared by the medical examiner marking each wound's location and depth, offered to illustrate her testimony.
A computer animation of the expert's opinion about the order of the wounds, with an instruction that it only illustrates her opinion.
oe: Correct. These prove nothing about the disputed issue and will mainly horrify the jury. That is the core of Bocharski.
Graphic, but strongly probative of premeditation, the disputed element. Rule 403 favors admission here.
An ordinary demonstrative aid that is probative and not inflammatory.
Under Serge, an animation that fairly reflects the expert's opinion is judged like other evidence. Being persuasive is not unfair prejudice.

q: In a robbery prosecution, the government's expert testifies that 1 in 50 local pickups are blue with a ladder rack, based on vehicle-registration data. He adds that 1 in 20 men in the area have red beards, a figure he says reflects his experience, and that 1 in 10 drivers wear orange caps, a figure the prosecutor suggested. He multiplies the figures and tells the jury that there is therefore "only a 1 in 10,000 chance the defendant is innocent." What is the strongest basis for excluding or striking this testimony?
o: Inputs lack foundation, independence is assumed, and frequency is mistaken for guilt.
Vehicle-registration data is hearsay, so any statistic built on it is inadmissible regardless of how the expert uses it.
Mathematical probability evidence invades the jury's province and is therefore inadmissible in criminal prosecutions.
Physical characteristics such as hair color are character traits, so using them to identify the robber violates Rule 404(a).
oe: Correct. Collins identified each of these flaws. The final step, treating a random-match frequency as the probability of innocence, is a serious logical error.
Experts can rely on data of a kind reasonably relied on in the field. The real defects are the method and the inference.
Collins disclaimed hostility to mathematics. Properly founded statistics, such as DNA match probabilities, are routinely admitted.
Physical descriptions are not character traits in the sense Rule 404 addresses.

q: In a federal civil fraud trial against two co-defendants, the court admits a letter written by Defendant A that is admissible against A but not against Defendant B. B's counsel makes no request about the letter. Later, after six bystanders have given consistent accounts of a disputed meeting, the plaintiff calls a seventh bystander with the same account. B objects. After a verdict against both defendants, B argues on appeal that the court erred by failing to instruct the jury about the letter. Which statement best describes the court's obligations?
o: The court could exclude the seventh account as needlessly cumulative, and it had no duty to give an instruction B never requested.
The court had to give a limiting instruction on its own initiative, because evidence admissible against one party must always be limited.
The court had to admit the seventh account, because relevant evidence corroborating a disputed meeting cannot be excluded as repetitive.
The court should have excluded the letter altogether, because research shows jurors cannot follow limiting instructions.
oe: Correct. Rule 403 lists needless cumulative evidence and wasted time. Rule 105 requires a limiting instruction only on timely request.
Rule 105 operates on request. A party that wants the protection has to ask for it.
Rule 403 expressly allows exclusion of needlessly cumulative evidence, even if it is relevant.
Research such as Wissler & Saks informs the 403 balance. It doesn't require exclusion whenever an instruction is available.

q: A homeowner is burned when a space heater tips over and keeps running. She sues the manufacturer on a strict-liability design-defect theory. After the incident, the manufacturer adds an automatic tip-over shutoff switch to the model. At trial, the manufacturer's engineer testifies that adding such a switch "would have made the heater shut off whenever it was bumped, so it couldn't be used safely in a home." For which purpose may the homeowner use the redesign?
o: To rebut the engineer's claim that a tip-over switch could not have been added without making the heater unusable.
To prove that the original design was defective, because Rule 407 protects only defendants sued for negligence.
To prove that the missing switch caused her burns, because causation is a purpose distinct from culpability.
To impeach the engineer's general statement on direct that his company always puts consumer safety first.
oe: Correct. The engineer put feasibility in dispute, and a permitted purpose 'if disputed' is available. The court should give a limiting instruction and may still weigh Rule 403.
Since the 1997 amendment, 407 expressly bars use to prove a defect in a product or its design.
Using the redesign to show that the earlier design caused harm is really proof of defect. Calling it causation doesn't avoid the rule.
Courts read the impeachment exception narrowly so it doesn't swallow the rule. A general statement about safety isn't enough.

q: A cyclist sues a bike shop, claiming that it negligently tightened a seat-post bolt during assembly. After the accident, the bicycle's manufacturer, which is not a party, recalls the model and replaces the bolt with a redesigned one. The cyclist offers the recall to show that the bolt was unsafe and that the shop should have caught the problem. How should the court analyze the shop's objection?
o: Rule 407 does not bar a measure taken by a nonparty, but the court may still exclude it under 403 as saying little about the shop's care.
Rule 407 bars the recall, because the rule is written in the passive voice and covers remedial measures taken by anyone.
The recall is admissible to prove the shop's negligence, because a manufacturer's recall is binding evidence that the product was defective.
The recall is admissible only if the manufacturer testifies, because otherwise the shop cannot cross-examine anyone about the redesign.
oe: Correct. Most circuits hold that 407 doesn't apply to third-party measures, because its policy targets defendants' incentives. Courts often find such evidence weak on the defendant's fault.
Courts have rejected this literal reading in favor of the rule's policy of encouraging defendants to make repairs.
Even if the recall shows the bolt design was flawed, it bears only weakly on whether the shop assembled the bike carelessly. Rule 403 still applies.
The ability to cross-examine is not the governing test. The questions are Rules 407 and 403.

q: A delivery driver slips on ice outside a warehouse and sues its owner. The owner's answer and its trial testimony both concede that it owned and controlled the loading area. After the fall, the owner installed heated mats. The driver offers the mats "to show the owner controlled the area," and, failing that, "to show heated mats were feasible." The owner has not claimed that any other precaution was impossible or impractical. How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it for both purposes, because control is conceded and feasibility has not been disputed.
Admit it to show control, because Rule 407 lists control as a permitted purpose without regard to whether it is contested.
Admit it to show feasibility, because a plaintiff may always show that a safer alternative existed in a negligence case.
Admit it for both purposes with a limiting instruction, because Rule 105 cures any risk that the jury will infer negligence.
oe: Correct. Ownership, control, and feasibility are permitted purposes only 'if disputed.' Neither is disputed here, so the only remaining use is to prove negligence, which the rule forbids.
The 2011 restyling makes clear that 'if disputed' applies to ownership, control, and feasibility alike.
Feasibility becomes a permitted purpose only when the defendant contests it.
A limiting instruction can't create a permitted purpose that doesn't exist.

q: A dog bites a jogger. At the scene, the owner says, "Let me pay your emergency-room bill. I knew he'd nipped the mail carrier last month." Two months later, after the jogger's lawyer demands $40,000, the owner's letter disputes the amount, offers $8,000, and adds, "Yes, he'd bitten before, but never this badly." In the jogger's negligence suit, which evidence may she use to prove that the owner knew of the dog's dangerous tendencies?
o: The owner's statement at the scene about the mail carrier, but not the payment offer or anything in the later letter.
The owner's statement at the scene and the admission in the letter, because Rule 408 protects only offers of money.
Nothing the owner said, because the scene statement accompanied an offer to pay that Rule 409 shields together with its context.
The admission in the letter only, because statements made after a demand are more deliberate and therefore more reliable.
oe: Correct. Rule 409 excludes only the offer to pay medical expenses, not statements made with it. The letter came during negotiation of a claim disputed as to amount, so 408 covers both the offer and the statements in it.
Rule 408 protects conduct and statements made during compromise negotiations, not just the offers themselves.
This reads 409 as broadly as 408. The Advisory Committee chose to protect only the offer itself.
Reliability isn't the test. The letter is a protected compromise communication.

q: A roofer invoices a homeowner $50,000. The homeowner emails: "Your work was excellent and I owe every penny, but cash is tight. Will you take $35,000 now as payment in full?" The roofer refuses. A month later the homeowner claims for the first time that the flashing leaks and refuses to pay anything. In the roofer's suit, he offers the email to prove the debt. How should the court rule?
o: Admit it, because when the email was sent there was no dispute about validity or amount, just a discount request.
Exclude the email, because any offer to accept less than the amount demanded is an attempt to compromise the claim.
Exclude the email, because the claim later became disputed and the protection applies to all communications about it.
Admit the email, but only to show the homeowner's bias, because Rule 408 permits that purpose even for protected offers.
oe: Correct. Rule 408 applies only to claims disputed as to validity or amount. An offer to discount an admitted debt doesn't implicate the rule's policy, and a dispute that arises later does not cover the earlier email.
The Advisory Committee Note says otherwise. The rule requires an actual dispute.
Coverage depends on whether a dispute existed when the communication was made.
There is no bias issue here. The email comes in as substantive proof because 408 doesn't apply at all.

q: Variation: The homeowner disputed the leaky flashing from the start, and at a mediation his representative said, "Our inspector found that only one section actually leaks." At trial, the homeowner's inspector testifies that the flashing leaks along the entire roofline. The roofer offers the mediation statement only to impeach the inspector. How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because Rule 408 bars using compromise statements to impeach by prior inconsistent statement or contradiction.
Admit it, because it is offered to impeach rather than to prove the validity or amount of the disputed claim.
Admit it, because the inspector did not make the statement and so cannot claim the protection of the compromise rule.
Admit it, because mediation sessions are formal proceedings rather than the private negotiations that Rule 408 covers.
oe: Correct. The 2006 amendment settled this. Allowing impeachment would chill the candor that settlement talks depend on, and it doesn't matter that the statement is used against a nonparty witness rather than the party who made it.
Rule 408(a) expressly lists impeachment by inconsistent statement or contradiction as a prohibited use.
The protection attaches to the negotiation statement itself, whoever is being contradicted.
Mediation is a classic setting for compromise negotiations under Rule 408.
pre: A roofer invoices a homeowner $50,000. The homeowner emails: "Your work was excellent and I owe every penny, but cash is tight. Will you take $35,000 now as payment in full?" The roofer refuses. A month later the homeowner claims for the first time that the flashing leaks and refuses to pay anything. In the roofer's suit, he offers the email to prove the debt. How should the court rule?

q: Two passengers are injured in the same crash and sue the driver separately. The driver settles with Passenger A for an unusually generous sum. At Passenger B's trial, Passenger A testifies for the driver that B distracted the driver just before the crash. B offers the settlement for two purposes: to show A's slant in the driver's favor, and to show that the driver must have been at fault because he paid A so much. Which use is permitted?
o: Only the first, to show A's bias, with an instruction that it cannot be used as proof of the driver's liability.
Only the second, because a settlement with a different claimant falls outside Rule 408 when offered to prove liability.
Both uses, because A's testimony opened the door to every fact about the settlement that bears on the case.
Neither use, because Rule 408 forbids evidence of any completed settlement whatever the purpose of the offer.
oe: Correct. Rule 408(b) allows proof of a witness's bias. Courts may apply 408 to third-party compromises offered to prove liability, which is the second use.
Every circuit that has addressed the issue lets courts exclude third-party compromises offered to prove liability, in order to protect settlement.
Bias is a limited purpose. Testifying doesn't make the settlement admissible to prove liability.
Rule 408(b) expressly allows other purposes, including bias.

q: A used-car dealer is prosecuted for odometer fraud. The prosecutor offers four statements to prove his guilt. Which may be admitted over his Rule 408 objection?
o: His admission made while negotiating a civil penalty with the attorney general's office.
His admission that he rolled back the odometer, made while negotiating a disputed refund with a defrauded buyer's private attorney.
His offer of $20,000 to the attorney general's office to end its civil penalty case, offered as evidence of consciousness of guilt.
His admission to the private attorney, offered only to contradict his trial testimony that he never touched any odometer.
oe: Correct. Rule 408(a)(2) allows statements from negotiations over a claim by a public office acting in its regulatory or enforcement capacity to be used in a later criminal case.
Statements in private civil compromise talks remain protected in later criminal cases when offered to prove liability.
Rule 408(a)(2) covers conduct and statements, not the offer itself. The offer remains barred as proof of liability.
Impeachment by contradiction is a prohibited use under Rule 408(a).

q: A defendant charged with bank fraud makes four incriminating statements before trial. None led to a guilty plea, and he signed no waiver. At trial, the government offers each statement. Which is protected by Rule 410?
o: His statement to an FBI agent whom the prosecutor had designated in writing to receive his proposal for a plea agreement.
His statement to a detective who promised to 'put in a good word' but had no authority from the prosecutor to negotiate.
His statement to a cellmate that he planned to offer the prosecutor information in exchange for a reduced charge.
His statement in open court during the colloquy for a guilty plea the court accepted and that he never withdrew.
oe: Correct. Rule 410(a)(4) covers discussions with an attorney for the prosecuting authority, including an agent the prosecutor has authorized to conduct them.
Bargaining with police who lack the prosecutor's authority isn't covered (Greene). The defendant's hope for a deal doesn't matter.
A statement to a private person is not a plea discussion with a prosecuting attorney.
Rule 410 covers withdrawn guilty pleas and statements tied to them. A plea that was accepted and never withdrawn falls outside it.

q: Before a proffer session, a defendant signs an agreement allowing the government to use his statements "to rebut any evidence or argument offered by or on behalf of the defendant that is inconsistent with them." In the session he admits he was at the warehouse on the night of the theft. At trial he does not testify, but in opening statement his lawyer tells the jury that the defendant "was never at that warehouse." What should the court do with the proffer statements?
o: Admit them to rebut the argument, because Rule 410's protections may be waived by a knowing and voluntary agreement.
Exclude them, because Rule 410 reflects a public policy favoring plea bargaining that defendants cannot waive.
Exclude them, because a waiver can be enforced only to impeach a defendant who testifies inconsistently on the stand.
Admit them only in a later perjury prosecution, because Rule 410 allows plea statements to be used only in that setting.
oe: Correct. Mezzanatto upheld waivers of 410. Many circuits enforce rebuttal waivers like this one, triggered by defense argument and not only by the defendant's testimony.
Mezzanatto rejected the claim that the rule cannot be waived.
The waiver's text reaches defense arguments as well. Mezzanatto approved an impeachment waiver, and courts have since enforced broader ones.
This confuses the 410(b)(2) exception with the separate route of waiver by agreement.

q: After a fatal crash, the driver faces criminal charges and a civil wrongful-death suit. The plaintiff in the civil suit offers four items against him. Which is admissible over a Rule 410 objection?
o: His guilty plea to vehicular manslaughter, which the court accepted and which he never sought to withdraw.
His earlier guilty plea to reckless driving, which the court allowed him to withdraw before sentencing.
His plea of nolo contendere to a related speeding charge, entered to avoid admitting fault for the crash.
His statements to the judge during the colloquy for the nolo plea, explaining what he remembered of the crash.
oe: Correct. Rule 410 excludes withdrawn guilty pleas and nolo pleas. An accepted guilty plea that stands is a party's admission and is outside the rule.
A withdrawn guilty plea is inadmissible against the person who made it, in civil and criminal cases alike.
Nolo pleas are inadmissible against the person who pleaded. Avoiding civil consequences is their purpose.
Rule 410(a)(3) also covers statements made in the plea proceedings for a nolo plea.

q: Before a first-degree murder trial, the prosecutor offers the defendant a plea to second-degree murder, and he refuses. At trial the defense offers the offer to suggest (1) that the prosecutor doubted she could prove premeditation and (2) that refusing the deal shows the defendant's belief in his own innocence. The government objects under Rule 410. Which response most accurately states the governing analysis?
o: Rule 410 protects only defendants, so admissibility turns on weak probative value and misleading effect under 403.
Rule 410 bars all evidence of plea discussions regardless of who offers it, so the court must exclude the offer.
Rule 410 is inapplicable and the offer is highly probative of innocence, so the court must admit it on the defendant's request.
Rule 410(b)(1)'s completeness exception requires admission, because the defendant participated in the same plea discussions.
oe: Correct. Rule 410 bars plea evidence 'against the defendant.' Courts generally exclude prosecutors' offers anyway, because offers reflect resources, risk, and strategy, and refusing one says little about innocence (Problem 2.8).
The text is one-directional: it protects the defendant who took part in the discussions.
The rule doesn't apply, but the evidence's weak probative value invites exclusion under 403.
Completeness applies only when another statement from the same discussions has already been introduced.

q: A pedestrian is struck by a landscaping truck and sues Rojas, claiming he owned the truck and employed its driver. Rojas denies both. Four uses of liability-insurance evidence are proposed. Which is permitted?
o: The pedestrian shows that Rojas bought the liability policy covering the truck, to prove that he owned it.
The pedestrian shows that Rojas was insured, to argue that a covered owner had less reason to supervise drivers carefully.
Rojas shows that he was uninsured, to argue that someone with no coverage had every reason to make sure his drivers were careful.
The pedestrian shows that Rojas was insured, so jurors will know that a large award will be paid by the carrier rather than by Rojas.
oe: Correct. Rule 411(b) permits insurance evidence to prove agency, ownership, or control when those facts are disputed, subject to 403 and a limiting instruction.
This uses insurance to prove negligent conduct, which Rule 411 forbids.

Rule 411 bars insurance evidence to prove whether a person acted negligently, which covers lack of insurance too and cuts both ways. The same logic is the strongest objection to the daycare defendant's offer in Problem 2.7.
This is the deep-pocket inference that Rule 411 is designed to prevent.

q: A father is charged with theft after store video shows his ten-year-old son, who was holding the father's open tote bag, slip five comics into it. The father paid for three other comics and carried the bag out. He claims he never saw what his son did. The State offers a fifteen-year-old police report showing that he was arrested, but never charged, after eating grapes in a grocery store. He told the officer he was tasting them before deciding whether to buy. The State argues that the incident shows intent and absence of mistake. How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because its only real path to intent runs through his character, and any slight value is outweighed under Rule 403.
Admit it, because intent and absence of mistake are listed purposes and the defendant has placed his knowledge in dispute.
Exclude it, because an arrest that never led to charges cannot be used as other-act evidence under Rule 404(b).
Admit it, because the evidence is relevant to intent under Rule 401, and relevant evidence is admissible under Rule 402.
oe: Correct. Openly eating sample grapes says nothing about whether he knew what his son put in the bag. The inference depends on 'he's a thief,' and remoteness and dissimilarity weigh heavily under 403.
Listing a purpose isn't enough. The inference must avoid character, and Rule 403 still applies.
Uncharged acts can qualify if a jury could find them under Huddleston's standard.
Relevance is a low bar, but Rule 404 is exactly the kind of 'other rule' that Rule 402 recognizes.
topic: Character and other acts — 404(b) after the MEE

q: Variation: Instead, the State offers testimony from another shop owner. Two months earlier, the same son put comics into the same tote bag. The owner stopped the father at the door, and the father laughed, said "He does that," and paid for them. How should the court rule?
o: Likely admit it to show knowledge and absence of mistake, subject to Rule 403 and a limiting instruction on request.
Exclude it, because evidence that the defendant previously left a store with unpaid goods shows only his propensity to steal.
Admit it for any purpose, because the earlier incident is so similar to the charged conduct that it bears directly on guilt.
Exclude it, because the earlier shop was not the victim of the charged theft and so the incident is irrelevant.
oe: Correct. Being warned about his son's habit makes his claim of ignorance less believable without relying on any character trait. Rule 105 lets him confine the jury's use of it.
The earlier incident proves he knew of the risk. That inference doesn't depend on his character.
Similarity doesn't remove the limits of 404(b). The jury may use it for knowledge, not for propensity.
Who the victim was is beside the point. The incident bears on the father's knowledge.

q: A defendant is charged with robbing a credit union. The robber wore an orange construction hard hat, handed the teller a demand note written on the back of a pizza coupon, and fled in a moving van stolen that morning. Identity is the only disputed issue. The government offers evidence of one other robbery. Which prior robbery has the strongest basis for admission to prove identity?
o: A robbery in which the defendant wore an orange hard hat, passed a note on a pizza coupon, and fled in a stolen moving van.
A robbery in which the defendant used a handgun, demanded cash from the teller drawer, and fled from the bank in a car.
A robbery of a branch of the same credit union, committed by the defendant in the same city one year earlier.
A robbery in which the defendant wore a mask, threatened a teller, and was convicted after a jury trial in state court.
oe: Correct. These shared features are idiosyncratic and together work as a signature. The inference is that 'it could not be anyone else's' (Trenkler).
These features are common to bank robberies. Commonplace similarities don't show identity (Pisari).
The same victim and city aren't distinctive. The inference that remains is propensity.
A conviction may make the act easier to prove, but it doesn't supply the distinctive similarity identity requires.
topic: Character and other acts — Identity / M.O.

q: Undercover video shows a man in a hooded jacket selling heroin. The defendant concedes that whoever made the sale knew it was heroin, but he says he is not the man in the video. The government offers his prior conviction for heroin distribution "to show his knowledge of the heroin trade, which makes it more likely that he is the seller." How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because knowledge is undisputed and the remaining path to identity runs through his propensity to deal drugs.
Admit it, because knowledge is a purpose listed in Rule 404(b)(2) and the government has said that it is offered for that purpose.
Admit it, because the defendant opened the door to his past by disputing identity, which permits rebuttal with similar acts.
Exclude it, but only because a prior drug conviction must be at least as recent as ten years to be admissible under Rule 404(b).
oe: Correct. When knowledge is conceded, labeling the evidence 'knowledge' only hides the inference that he dealt before and so dealt again (Drug Seller, Problem 3.2).
Naming a purpose doesn't validate the chain of reasoning. Ask whether the chain avoids character.
Disputing identity doesn't open a door to propensity. Identity evidence needs a signature-level link.
Rule 404(b) has no ten-year limit. Remoteness goes to the 403 balance.
topic: Character and other acts — Knowledge → identity

q: Variation: In a drug case, it is disputed whether the defendant lived in the apartment where the drugs were found. Police also found illegal lottery slips there. The government offers his conviction for running a numbers game six years ago, reasoning that the occupant gambled, the defendant gambled six years ago, and so he is likely the occupant. How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because inferring present gambling from gambling six years ago is itself a propensity inference.
Admit it, because the gambling slips connect the occupant to an activity that the defendant has been convicted of before.
Admit it as habit evidence, because running a numbers game is a regular commercial practice that persists over time.
Admit it, because gambling is not a violent offense and therefore creates little risk of unfair prejudice to the defendant.
oe: Correct. Break the chain into steps and the middle step, 'gambled then, so gambles now,' is propensity reasoning (Lottery Lists, Problem 3.8).
That connection works only through the inference that he still gambles, which is a propensity inference.
An illegal business years earlier is not the reflexive, specific response that habit requires.
Low prejudice doesn't cure a forbidden inference. Rule 404(b) is a categorical bar on propensity use.
topic: Character and other acts — Lottery-list chain
pre: Undercover video shows a man in a hooded jacket selling heroin. The defendant concedes that whoever made the sale knew it was heroin, but he says he is not the man in the video. The government offers his prior conviction for heroin distribution "to show his knowledge of the heroin trade, which makes it more likely that he is the seller." How should the court rule?

q: A defendant is charged with a bank robbery in which the robber wore a distinctive knitted mask with cut-out eyes. The government offers a witness who says that two weeks later she unmasked an intruder wearing the same kind of mask in her home and recognized him as the defendant. The defendant was tried for that home invasion and acquitted. Which statement best describes how the court should analyze the evidence?
o: It may be admitted if a jury could reasonably find by a preponderance that he was the intruder, and the acquittal does not bar it.
It must be excluded, because collateral estoppel prevents the government from relitigating conduct a jury has already acquitted.
It may be admitted only if the judge first finds by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant was the intruder.
It may be admitted, but the jury may not learn that he was acquitted, because the acquittal would confuse the issues.
oe: Correct. Huddleston applies the 104(b) sufficiency standard, and Dowling holds that an acquittal shows only reasonable doubt. The defense may tell the jury about the acquittal, and 403 still applies.
Dowling rejected this argument because the two proceedings use different standards of proof.
Huddleston rejected a heightened preliminary finding by the judge.
Courts generally allow the defense to tell the jury about the acquittal to reduce prejudice.
topic: Character and other acts — Huddleston · Dowling

q: A defendant is charged with shooting a state trooper during a traffic stop. When stopped, he had an outstanding warrant for an aggravated child-sexual-abuse charge. The government gives written notice before trial that it will offer the warrant to show motive. How should the court rule?
o: Admit evidence that he was wanted on a serious felony warrant, but exclude the nature of the underlying charge under Rule 403.
Admit the warrant and the nature of the underlying charge, because the full details show how badly he wanted to avoid arrest.
Exclude the warrant entirely, because evidence that a defendant faced another serious charge necessarily invites propensity reasoning.
Admit the warrant only if he had been convicted of the underlying charge, because motive cannot rest on unproven accusations.
oe: Correct. Peltier treats a pending warrant as a non-character motive to avoid arrest. The nature of the charge adds little to that motive and great prejudice, so sanitizing it is the right tool. Notice under 404(b)(3) was given.
The marginal value of the charge's nature is small, and its inflammatory effect is large. That is a classic case for 403 trimming.
The warrant supplies a reason to shoot that doesn't depend on character. That makes it a proper motive use.
His motive comes from the warrant's existence, not from whether he was guilty of the underlying charge.
topic: Character and other acts — Motive · notice

q: Variation: A white officer is prosecuted for the fatal shooting of a Black motorist during a traffic stop. The State offers evidence that he wore a Confederate-flag T-shirt under his uniform that day, arguing that it shows racial animus as a motive. What is the court's most important inquiry?
o: Whether the shirt supports a real inference of animus toward this motorist that supplies a motive, weighed against its prejudice.
Whether the officer chose the shirt knowingly, because any voluntary display of a symbol is admissible as evidence of intent.
Whether clothing is protected expression, because protected expression may never be offered against a criminal defendant.
Whether the officer wore the shirt regularly on duty, because regular wearing would make it admissible as habit evidence.
oe: Correct. Motive is a legitimate non-propensity purpose only if the chain holds. The court must then weigh inflammatory effect under 403 (Confederate Flag, Problem 3.4).
Knowing the shirt was chosen doesn't by itself establish a motive. The court still has to evaluate the chain of inference and Rule 403.
Expression can be evidence of motive or intent. There is no categorical bar.
Wearing a shirt is not the kind of behavior habit evidence covers, and habit isn't the theory being offered.
topic: Character and other acts — Motive vs. propensity
