q: A defendant is charged with possessing a revolver with an obliterated serial number, found in a backpack in his bedroom. He claims it belonged to a cousin. His former fiancée will testify that a year earlier she saw him load a single round into that same revolver, spin the cylinder, point it at her head, and pull the trigger. Which ruling is best?
o: Permit her to say she saw him load, spin, and fire that revolver, but bar any mention that he pointed it at her.
Admit her full account, because narrative integrity requires that a witness be allowed to describe the incident as she lived it.
Exclude her account entirely, because any earlier act involving a firearm shows the defendant's propensity for gun violence.
Exclude her account, because possession a year earlier says nothing about who possessed the revolver when it was found.
oe: Correct. Her account proves he possessed this gun, which is not a character purpose. Removing the threat reduces 403 prejudice while keeping the narrative coherent (Hite).
Narrative concerns don't override 403. Courts routinely sanitize details that add prejudice but little proof.
The act proves possession of this specific gun, which is a proper non-character use.
Possession earlier makes possession later more probable, especially given the cousin defense.
topic: Character and other acts — Res gestae · 403

q: A landlord is charged with arson after a fire in one of his buildings. He says that faulty wiring caused it. The government offers evidence that two other buildings he owned burned in the past four years, that he blamed faulty wiring both times, and that each fire came within weeks of an insurance increase. He was never charged for the earlier fires. Which theory most persuasively supports admission?
o: Three similar fires, each followed by a similar claim, are unlikely to be innocent electrical accidents, which rebuts his claim.
The earlier fires show that he is the kind of landlord willing to destroy property to collect insurance money.
The earlier fires are admissible as habit, because a regular pattern of fires followed by claims is a routine business practice.
The earlier fires are admissible because he was never charged, so the jury may evaluate them without prejudice from a conviction.
oe: Correct. Absence of accident and the doctrine of chances (Rex v. Smith; Problem 3.12) rest on improbability. Huddleston's standard applies to the earlier fires, and 403 remains.
That is the propensity inference that Rule 404(a) bars.
Setting fires is not a reflexive, specific response to a recurring situation.
Never being charged doesn't make the evidence admissible. If anything, it makes the acts harder to prove.
topic: Character and other acts — Absence of accident · chances

q: Variation: The landlord does not claim accident. He concedes the fire was arson but says a disgruntled former tenant set it. The government offers the same two earlier fires. How does the analysis change?
o: The accident theory falls away, and unless the fires share signature features that show identity, Rule 403 likely excludes them.
Nothing changes, because the doctrine of chances applies whenever a defendant has been connected to several similar events.
The fires become more admissible, because blaming a third party puts his character for honesty directly at issue.
The fires become admissible as reverse 404(b) evidence, because the defense has pointed the jury toward someone else.
oe: Correct. Purposes depend on what is actually disputed. With identity at issue, the government needs distinctive similarity, not just a pattern of fires.
Chances works by rebutting a claim of innocent coincidence. Here the defendant concedes the fire was arson.
Denying guilt doesn't put character at issue under 404(a)(2) or 405(b).
Reverse 404(b) concerns evidence the defendant offers about third parties. It has nothing to do with this offer.
topic: Character and other acts — When accident isn't claimed
pre: A landlord is charged with arson after a fire in one of his buildings. He says that faulty wiring caused it. The government offers evidence that two other buildings he owned burned in the past four years, that he blamed faulty wiring both times, and that each fire came within weeks of an insurance increase. He was never charged for the earlier fires. Which theory most persuasively supports admission?

q: In a state that follows the federal rules but has no counterpart to Rules 413–415, a stepfather is charged with sexually abusing his stepdaughter. The State offers evidence that years earlier he groomed and abused a different child in the same way and argues that the incidents show a "common plan or scheme." Under the approach of State v. Kirsch, what must the State show?
o: An overarching scheme of which each act is a part, not merely that the acts were committed in a similar way.
That each earlier act was itself planned in advance rather than committed on impulse, which shows a deliberate design.
That the earlier acts closely resemble the charged acts, which makes it likely the defendant followed the same plan.
Nothing beyond the defendant's identity as the actor, because sexual offenses against children are always admissible as plan.
oe: Correct. Kirsch rejects 'plan' when the State only shows that each crime was planned the same way. Raeder argues that domestic violence often fits a linked-chain plan.
Planning each act separately isn't a common plan. That is propensity under another name.
Similarity alone is the M.O. route and requires distinctiveness. It isn't plan.
Without a Rule 414 counterpart, the State has to fit a real 404(b) purpose.
topic: Character and other acts — Common plan (Kirsch)

q: A defendant is charged with a shooting on Ninth Street with a .40-caliber pistol. The prosecution offers one of four items. Which has the strongest basis for admission?
o: A verse he posted two days after the shooting describing "dropping a man on Ninth with the forty," matching the crime's details.
A box of three handguns, none of them .40-caliber, found in his closet, offered to show he was a man ready to shoot.
Violent lyrics he wrote four years earlier about shootings in general, offered to show his familiarity with gun violence.
His conviction for an unrelated assault three years earlier, offered to show his willingness to use force against others.
oe: Correct. A specific match to the charged crime turns lyrics into something close to an admission. Skinner requires that strong nexus.
Zackowitz condemns exactly this: weapons unconnected to the crime offered to show a dangerous character.
Without a nexus to the crime, the lyrics mainly suggest violent character, and 403 weighs heavily (Skinner).
This is pure propensity, barred by 404(a)(1).
topic: Character and other acts — Zackowitz · lyrics

q: Drugs are found in an apartment shared by the defendant and his roommate. The defendant claims the drugs were the roommate's. He offers evidence about the roommate. Which offer has the strongest basis for admission?
o: Last month the roommate sold drugs from the same apartment in the same uncommon stamped bags found in this seizure.
The roommate has two prior convictions for possession, offered to show that he is the kind of person who keeps drugs at home.
The roommate has a reputation in the neighborhood as a drug user, offered to show that he more likely owned the drugs.
The roommate once lied to police about his address, offered to show he would hide drugs in another person's home.
oe: Correct. When a defendant offers a third person's other acts, courts may require less similarity (Stevens). This evidence ties the roommate to these drugs through specific features.
Williams: reverse 404(b) is not a license for propensity. Rule 404(b) protects any person.
This is character to show conduct, barred by 404(a)(1) no matter who offers it.
The inference runs through a dishonest character. It isn't a specific link to these drugs.

q: A defendant charged with wire fraud calls a longtime neighbor, who testifies that the defendant has an excellent reputation for honesty. The prosecutor has good-faith bases for each of the following. Which is least likely to be permitted?
o: Calling a bank investigator to prove the 2018 forgery after the neighbor denies hearing of it.
Asking the neighbor, "Have you heard that the defendant was arrested in 2018 for forging loan documents?"
Calling a former business partner to give an opinion that the defendant is a dishonest person.
Asking the neighbor, "Have you heard that the defendant was fired in 2020 for falsifying expense reports?"
oe: Correct, this is not permitted. Rule 405(a) allows inquiry into specific acts on cross, but not extrinsic proof of the act to rebut character.
Proper. Michelson allows questions about arrests to test whether the witness really knows the defendant's reputation.
Proper. Once the defendant offers a pertinent trait, the prosecution may rebut it with reputation or opinion evidence.
Proper. Michelson-style cross on relevant specific acts, with a limiting instruction.

q: A defendant is charged with assault with a deadly weapon after a bar fight. The victim survived. The defendant testifies that the victim swung first, and he calls a witness who says the victim has a reputation for violence. The prosecution then offers three items in rebuttal: (i) the victim's reputation for peacefulness, (ii) the defendant's reputation for violence, and (iii) a witness who saw the defendant start a different bar fight last year. Which may be admitted?
o: (i) and (ii), but not (iii).
(i) only.
(ii) and (iii), but not (i).
(i), (ii), and (iii).
oe: Correct. Attacking the victim's trait permits rebuttal of that trait and evidence of the same trait in the accused (404(a)(2)(B)). Rule 405(a) limits both to reputation or opinion, so extrinsic proof of the specific bar fight is barred.
Under 404(a)(2)(B)(ii), the defendant's attack on the victim's violence also opens the door to the defendant's own violence.
The victim's peacefulness is the most direct rebuttal. The specific bar fight is not an allowed form of proof.
Specific instances can't be proved extrinsically to show character when character is not an essential element.

q: Variation: Same bar fight and assault charge, but the defendant offers no character evidence. He only testifies that the victim swung first. The prosecution offers the victim's reputation for peacefulness. How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because the first-aggressor route for a victim's peacefulness applies only in homicide cases.
Admit it, because evidence that the victim was the first aggressor always permits rebuttal with the victim's peacefulness.
Admit it, because the defendant's testimony put his own character for peacefulness directly at issue.
Exclude it, because a victim's character may be proved only through specific instances of conduct.
oe: Correct. Rule 404(a)(2)(C) is limited to homicide. In other cases the door opens only if the defendant offers evidence of the victim's character.
That is true only in homicide cases, where the victim can't testify.
Testifying about events doesn't put character in issue. Saying 'I'm peaceful' would.
Reputation or opinion is the ordinary method under 405(a).
topic: Character and other acts — Homicide-only rule
pre: A defendant is charged with assault with a deadly weapon after a bar fight. The victim survived. The defendant testifies that the victim swung first, and he calls a witness who says the victim has a reputation for violence. The prosecution then offers three items in rebuttal: (i) the victim's reputation for peacefulness, (ii) the defendant's reputation for violence, and (iii) a witness who saw the defendant start a different bar fight last year. Which may be admitted?

q: A defendant is charged with assaulting a man during a parking-lot fight and claims self-defense. The man testifies for the prosecution that the defendant attacked without provocation. Only after the fight did the defendant learn that the man had a six-year-old felony conviction for stabbing a stranger. Which use of the conviction is most likely proper?
o: Impeaching the man's credibility as a witness under Rule 609, with an instruction that it does not show who attacked first.
Proving the man's violent character to show he attacked first, because self-defense puts the victim's character in issue.
Showing the defendant's reasonable fear, because the stabbing makes it more likely that a person would fear this man.
Proving the man's violent character through the conviction, because a conviction is more reliable than reputation testimony.
oe: Correct. The man testified, so his felony conviction is subject to 609(a)(1)(A) and ordinary 403 balancing, but only for credibility.
Character is not an essential element of self-defense, so 405(b) doesn't apply. Specific acts can't prove the victim's character (Keiser).
The defendant didn't know about the stabbing at the time of the fight, so it couldn't have affected his fear (compare James, Problem 3.18).
Reliability doesn't change the method. Rule 405(a) still limits proof to reputation or opinion.
topic: Character and other acts — Keiser · state of mind · 609

q: A defendant charged with tax evasion testifies on direct: "I've never cheated anyone out of a dime in my life. I'm an honest person." He also calls a coworker who testifies that he has a reputation as a peaceful, gentle man. What follows?
o: His own testimony offered honesty, which the State may rebut, but peacefulness is not a pertinent trait here.
Neither statement opens any door, because a defendant's own testimony and a coworker's reputation testimony cannot put character in issue.
Both items are admissible, and the State may now offer evidence of any bad character trait the defendant has.
The honesty statement must be struck as bolstering, because a witness may not support his own credibility before it is attacked.
oe: Correct. Calling oneself honest is character evidence of a pertinent trait, which opens rebuttal ('I Wouldn't Shoot Anybody', Problem 3.16). Peacefulness is irrelevant to tax evasion.
A defendant's description of his own character is character evidence, and it opens the door.
Rebuttal is limited to the trait that was offered. Peacefulness was not pertinent in the first place.
Bolstering concerns credibility under 608. This statement is substantive character evidence under 404(a)(2)(A).
topic: Character and other acts — Pertinence · opening the door

q: A warehouse worker is crushed when a loading-dock gate drops. The disputed issue is whether the night supervisor engaged the gate's safety lock when he closed up that night. No one remembers that night. The company offers testimony to show that he did. Which is the best evidence?
o: A guard who, for two years, watched the supervisor flip the lock and tug the gate twice every time he closed the dock at night.
The safety manager's testimony that company policy required every supervisor to engage the lock, though she never observed closings.
Coworkers who describe the supervisor as an extremely careful, safety-minded person who never cuts corners.
A guard who saw the supervisor engage the lock on several occasions when inspectors were visiting the warehouse.
oe: Correct. A specific physical response to the same recurring situation, observed regularly, is habit under Rule 406. It's admissible even without corroboration or an eyewitness to that night.
A policy shows what should happen, not what this person regularly did.
That is character evidence of general carefulness, barred by 404(a)(1) in civil cases.
Behavior when inspectors are present is neither routine nor representative of ordinary closings.

q: Variation: In a malpractice case, a physician denies ever prescribing steroids to the decedent and says someone else must have. The estate offers eight former patients who each testify that, over many years, the physician gave them steroid pills while telling them the pills were antihistamines. What is the strongest basis for admission?
o: Habit or routine practice, because years of the same specific prescribing conduct show what he did with this patient.
Character for dishonesty, because the physician's misrepresentations to patients show the kind of doctor he is.
Modus operandi, because a distinctive signature proves that he, rather than some other physician, prescribed the steroids.
Impeachment, because the testimony contradicts his denial and may be considered only on the question of his credibility.
oe: Correct. Weil v. Seltzer (Problem 3.20) admitted this as habit. The consistency and specificity of the practice is the key.
Character to show conduct is barred in a civil case.
Identity framing is possible, but the court treated this as habit, which is the stronger fit.
The evidence comes in as substantive proof under 406, not merely to impeach.
topic: Character and other acts — Routine practice (Weil v. Seltzer)
pre: A warehouse worker is crushed when a loading-dock gate drops. The disputed issue is whether the night supervisor engaged the gate's safety lock when he closed up that night. No one remembers that night. The company offers testimony to show that he did. Which is the best evidence?

q: A bus passenger is injured in a crash. She sues the driver for negligence and the bus company for negligent retention, which requires proof that the driver was unfit and that the company knew or should have known it. Before the accident, three dispatchers had reported to the company in writing that the driver was drinking on breaks. The passenger offers the reports against both defendants. Which ruling is best?
o: Admit against the company on fitness and notice, with an instruction against conformity use.
Admit the reports against both defendants for all purposes, because the same drinking is relevant to both claims in the case.
Exclude the reports entirely, because evidence of past drinking is character evidence barred in civil cases.
Admit the reports only after the passenger first offers reputation testimony that the driver is a heavy drinker.
oe: Correct. The driver's unfitness is an essential element of the retention claim (405(b)), and the reports prove the company's notice (Henthorne, Problem 3.3). Using them to show conduct on the accident day is propensity, and Rule 105 confines that use.
Relevance to one claim doesn't permit the forbidden inference on the other claim.
When character is an element or notice is at issue, the evidence serves a non-propensity purpose.
When a trait is an essential element, Rule 405(b) allows specific instances directly. No reputation evidence is required first.

q: Variation: In the same suit, the driver offers his pastor's testimony that he has a reputation for sobriety and careful driving. How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because the 404(a)(2) exceptions belong to criminal defendants and do not apply in civil cases.
Admit it, because the passenger's evidence of drinking opened the door to rebuttal with the driver's good character.
Admit it, because sobriety is a pertinent trait when the opposing party alleges that the defendant was drinking.
Admit it as habit, because sobriety and careful driving are regular practices rather than character traits.
oe: Correct. The 'mercy rule' doesn't apply in civil cases, even when the conduct resembles a crime.
The passenger's evidence came in for a permitted purpose. That doesn't open a character door in a civil case.
Pertinence matters only within 404(a)(2), which is limited to criminal cases.
These are general dispositions, not specific reflexive responses.
topic: Character and other acts — Civil character
pre: A bus passenger is injured in a crash. She sues the driver for negligence and the bus company for negligent retention, which requires proof that the driver was unfit and that the company knew or should have known it. Before the accident, three dispatchers had reported to the company in writing that the driver was drinking on breaks. The passenger offers the reports against both defendants. Which ruling is best?

q: A gynecologist is federally charged with sexually abusing two patients during examinations. After timely notice, the government offers four other patients who say he touched them in similar ways. None of their allegations was charged. The defense contends that the jury will get lost in expert disputes over which examination techniques were medically appropriate. Which statement best describes the court's approach?
o: Rule 413 permits propensity use, but ordinary 403 applies, including for confusion.
The evidence must be admitted, because Rule 413 evidence is exempt from Rule 403 balancing in sexual-assault prosecutions.
The evidence is admissible only for a 404(b) purpose such as plan, because propensity is never a permissible use.
The evidence may be excluded only for unfair prejudice, because confusion of the issues is not a ground for excluding 413 evidence.
oe: Correct. Guardia affirmed exclusion of this kind of evidence under ordinary 403, with no special presumption toward admission.
Rule 403 applies to all evidence, including evidence offered under 413.
Rule 413 expressly allows the jury to consider the evidence 'on any matter to which it is relevant,' including propensity.
All of 403's grounds remain available, including confusion of the issues.
topic: Character and other acts — FRE 413 · Guardia

q: Variation: (a) In a federal child-molestation prosecution, the defendant argues that admitting his past molestation of other children violates due process. (b) Separately, one of the patients in the gynecologist case sues him civilly for battery and offers the other patients' accounts. Which statement is correct?
o: (a) fails, because courts including Mound upheld Rule 414, and (b) may proceed under Rule 415, subject to Rule 403.
(a) succeeds, because propensity evidence offered by the prosecution always violates due process, and (b) fails as well.
(a) fails, but (b) is barred, because Rules 413 through 415 apply only when the government is the proponent.
(a) fails, but (b) is governed by Rule 412, because the civil case involves alleged sexual misconduct.
oe: Correct. The due-process challenges failed. Rule 415 extends 413 and 414 to civil claims based on sexual assault or child molestation.
Courts have consistently rejected that challenge.
Rule 415 is expressly a civil rule.
Rule 412 protects victims' sexual history. It doesn't govern a defendant's other assaults.
pre: A gynecologist is federally charged with sexually abusing two patients during examinations. After timely notice, the government offers four other patients who say he touched them in similar ways. None of their allegations was charged. The defense contends that the jury will get lost in expert disputes over which examination techniques were medically appropriate. Which statement best describes the court's approach?

q: In a civil collision suit, the plaintiff calls an eyewitness who unexpectedly testifies that the light was green for the defendant. The plaintiff then proposes four lines of evidence. Which is admissible?
o: Evidence that the eyewitness had left her prescription glasses at home that night and could not see the signal clearly.
A neighbor's testimony that the eyewitness has an excellent reputation for truthfulness, offered before any attack on her.
A neighbor's testimony that the eyewitness has a reputation for being a peaceful and law-abiding person.
The plaintiff's questions to the eyewitness about her once returning a lost wallet full of cash to its owner.
oe: Correct. Rule 607 lets a party impeach its own witness. Attacking her perception ('that's an error') is governed only by 401 and 403.
This is bolstering. Support under 608(a) comes only after a character attack, and the plaintiff wants to undercut her, not support her.
Peacefulness doesn't bear on credibility. Rule 608(a) is limited to truthfulness (Bar Fight, Problem 4.1).
Specific good acts to support truthfulness aren't allowed on direct, and her truthfulness hasn't been attacked.

q: A police officer is the only witness tying the defendant to a gun. Defense counsel has a state motor-vehicle record, which is inadmissible hearsay, showing that the officer's license was suspended and that he failed to report the suspension to his department as policy required. Which step may the defense take?
o: Ask the officer on cross whether he hid his license suspension from his department, relying on the record as a good-faith basis.
Offer the motor-vehicle record as an exhibit after the officer denies the suspension, to prove that he concealed it.
Read aloud from the record while asking, "Doesn't this official document say you concealed your suspension?"
Ask the officer whether he has failed to pay child support, because any violation of a legal duty bears on truthfulness.
oe: Correct. Concealment is probative of untruthfulness. A good-faith basis for the question need not be admissible evidence (Whitmore reversed the trial court for barring this cross).
Rule 608(b) bars extrinsic evidence of the act. The lawyer must take the answer.
Reading the document to the jury brings it in as extrinsic evidence through the back door. That is improper.
Nonpayment of child support isn't probative of truthfulness in itself.

q: A defense witness testifies that the defendant was with him at the time of a robbery. On cross, the prosecutor asks whether the witness and the defendant belong to a secret prison organization whose members are sworn to lie, steal, and kill for one another. The witness denies it. The prosecutor then calls a former member to describe the organization and identify both men as members. What is the strongest basis for admitting the former member's testimony?
o: It shows the witness's bias toward the defendant, and bias is never collateral, so extrinsic proof is allowed despite the denial.
It shows the witness's untruthful character through a specific act, which Rule 608(b) permits after the witness denies it.
It shows the defendant's motive under Rule 404(b), because membership explains why he would commit the robbery.
It contradicts the witness's denial, and contradiction on any point he denies may be proved with extrinsic evidence.
oe: Correct. Abel admitted this evidence. The organization's tenets also reflect on character, but the bias purpose controls, and 608(b) doesn't bar it.
Rule 608(b) does the opposite. It bars extrinsic proof of specific acts offered for truthfulness.
The evidence is offered to impeach the witness, not to prove the defendant's motive.
Contradiction on a collateral matter is subject to 403. Bias is the reason this proof comes in.

q: Variation: A cooperating witness who has been promised probation testifies that the defendant ran the drug lab. The defense offers two witnesses: one says she once falsely accused him of drug crimes to divert police attention from herself, and the other says she threatened to report him to drug agents unless he fixed her car for free. How should the court rule?
o: Admit both as evidence of a motive to make self-serving accusations, which is bias evidence outside 608(b)'s extrinsic bar.
Exclude both, because they are specific instances of untruthfulness, and Rule 608(b) limits the defense to cross-examination.
Admit both, but only in the form of reputation evidence about her character for truthfulness under Rule 608(a).
Exclude both under Rule 404(a)(1), because they show her propensity to make accusations against others.
oe: Correct. The acts show a pattern of using accusations for personal advantage, which is her motive here. Bias and motive are never collateral (Selfish Lies, Problem 4.9).
This treats the evidence only as character evidence. Its main purpose is bias and motive.
That would change the evidence's form for no reason. The specific acts come in because they show bias.
The inference isn't 'she accuses people.' It's 'she accuses people when it benefits her, and it benefits her now.' That is motive.
pre: A defense witness testifies that the defendant was with him at the time of a robbery. On cross, the prosecutor asks whether the witness and the defendant belong to a secret prison organization whose members are sworn to lie, steal, and kill for one another. The witness denies it. The prosecutor then calls a former member to describe the organization and identify both men as members. What is the strongest basis for admitting the former member's testimony?

q: Four prosecution witnesses are impeached in different ways. As to which witness may the prosecution now offer opinion testimony that the witness is a truthful person?
o: A witness impeached with a prior conviction for making a false statement on a federal loan application.
A witness shown on cross to be receiving immunity and a reduced sentence in exchange for her testimony.
A witness contradicted by a weather report on whether it was raining on the night she says she saw the defendant.
A witness confronted with a prior statement giving a slightly different time for the meeting she described.
oe: Correct. Impeachment under 609(a)(2) attacks character for truthfulness, which opens the door to rehabilitation under 608(a).
Bias suggests a reason to lie in this case, not a bad character. Rehabilitation with character evidence isn't allowed (Problem 4.6(1)).
A single contradiction suggests error, not a character attack, unless it is pervasive (Problem 4.6(2)).
Inconsistency alone generally doesn't attack character for truthfulness.

q: In a federal benefits-fraud trial, the victim is the government's key witness. Consider each proposed character witness separately. Which testimony about the victim's truthfulness is most likely admissible?
o: After the defense calls her a liar in its case, a coworker of six years testifies that, in his opinion, she is very truthful.
Before any attack, two longtime friends testify that she has always been scrupulously honest in her dealings with them.
After an attack, a former neighbor who moved away eight years ago describes her reputation in that old neighborhood.
After an attack, a witness describes her reputation among 'the courthouse community' based on talks with three lawyers.
oe: Correct. Once she is attacked, opinion rehabilitation is proper, and six years of current contact is an adequate foundation.
This is bolstering before any attack, which is impermissible (Bonner, Problem 4.7). Corroborating the facts of her testimony would be a different matter.
A reputation that is too remote in time lacks foundation (Whitmore).
A handful of conversations in a narrow circle is a weak foundation for reputation evidence (Whitmore).

q: An alibi witness testifies that she remembers dining with the defendant on the night of the crime because it was her birthday dinner at the Circle Deli. The prosecution has four pieces of extrinsic evidence. Which is the court most likely to admit?
o: The deli owner's testimony that the deli was closed all that day for a holiday, so no one dined there.
Her birth certificate showing that her birthday is in a different month, offered to show she is mistaken about the occasion.
A waiter's testimony that she ordered soup, not the steak she described, at a dinner that both agree took place.
A friend's testimony that she once lied about her age to get into a nightclub, offered to show she is untruthful.
oe: Correct. This goes to the core of the alibi itself, whether the dinner could have happened, so it isn't collateral.
This contradicts a detail about why she remembers the night. Courts often exclude such collateral points under 403 as a waste of time.
A trivial collateral contradiction. The court may exclude extrinsic proof of it.
Extrinsic proof of a specific lie is barred by 608(b).

q: In a federal criminal trial, four convictions are offered to impeach four different witnesses. Which one is governed by ordinary Rule 403 balancing?
o: A prosecution witness's robbery conviction from twelve years ago, for which he was released from prison nine years ago.
The testifying defendant's robbery conviction from three years ago, for which he served two years in prison.
A defense witness's forgery conviction from fifteen years ago, for which she paid a fine and served no time.
A defense witness's juvenile adjudication for theft, offered by the prosecution to show that he is untruthful.
oe: Correct. Ten years runs from the later of conviction or release. Nine years since release keeps it under 609(a)(1)(A), with ordinary 403 balancing for a non-accused witness.
For the accused, 609(a)(1)(B) applies: probative value must outweigh prejudicial effect to the defendant.
More than ten years old, so 609(b)'s reverse-403 test and notice requirement apply, even to crimen falsi.
Rule 609(d) allows juvenile adjudications only when necessary to determine guilt fairly, which is a stricter test.

q: A civil plaintiff testifies, and the defendant offers four misdemeanor convictions, each punishable by less than a year, to impeach her. Which must the court admit without any balancing?
o: Theft by deception, defined as obtaining property by creating a false impression of fact.
Shoplifting, where the evidence showed she hid merchandise under her coat before walking out.
Tampering with a utility meter under a statute defining the crime as a form of theft of services.
Possession of stolen property, where she claimed at trial that she believed the goods were legitimate.
oe: Correct. The elements require a deceptive act, which makes it crimen falsi. Rule 609(a)(2) admission is automatic.
Concealment is part of the conduct but not an element. Theft offenses aren't crimen falsi (Meter Fixing, Problem 4.5).
Theft is not crimen falsi, however sneaky the method.
Neither knowing possession nor a failed defense amounts to a dishonest act as an element.

q: In four separate federal trials, the judge rules before trial that the defendant's prior fraud conviction will be admitted under Rule 609 if he testifies. Each defendant is convicted and appeals that ruling. Which defendant has preserved the claim for appellate review?
o: The defendant who testified, did not mention it himself, and was impeached with it over objection.
The defendant who chose not to testify because the ruling made the risk of impeachment too great.
The defendant who testified and disclosed the conviction on direct examination to take the sting out of it.
The defendant who testified after the government said it might not use the conviction, and it never did.
oe: Correct. He testified, as Luce requires, and didn't introduce the conviction himself, so Ohler doesn't apply.
Luce: without testimony, a reviewing court can't assess the harm, so the claim isn't preserved.
Ohler: bringing out the conviction himself waives the objection.
There's no harm to review when the conviction was never used.

q: A defendant charged with cocaine distribution has a prior conviction for possession of cocaine for sale. The court excludes it from the government's case in chief under Rules 404(b) and 403. The defendant then testifies and denies the sale. The government offers the same conviction under Rule 609. Which statement is correct?
o: Rule 609(a)(1)(B) applies separately, and any admission is limited to credibility.
The 404(b) ruling controls, so the conviction is inadmissible for any purpose during the rest of the trial.
By testifying, the defendant made the conviction admissible as substantive proof that he sold cocaine again.
The conviction must be admitted, because a drug-distribution conviction is automatically admissible to impeach.
oe: Correct. Different purposes call for different tests (Weighing Tests, Problem 4.4). The similarity of the crimes weighs against admission under the Gordon factors.
An earlier exclusion for one purpose doesn't decide a separate rule's test for a different purpose.
Testifying opens the door to impeachment, not to propensity.
Only crimen falsi convictions are admitted automatically. Drug crimes go through the 609(a)(1) balancing tests.

q: Variation: The court admits the conviction under 609. The defense asks that the jury hear only that he has "a felony conviction." Separately, the prosecutor asks for leave to call a witness who will say that the defendant has a reputation for sexual immorality. Which statement is correct?
o: The court has discretion to withhold the name of the crime, though jurors generally learn it, and the immorality reputation is barred.
The court must withhold the name under Old Chief, and the immorality reputation is admissible because it bears on credibility.
The court must always name the crime, and the immorality reputation is admissible to rebut the defendant's denial.
The court may disclose neither the name nor the fact of conviction, and the reputation is admissible only if he testifies.
oe: Correct. Estrada endorses the general practice of naming the crime while leaving discretion. Rule 608(a) limits character impeachment to truthfulness, which rejects the old approach seen in Sibley.
Old Chief concerns status elements, not impeachment, and chastity isn't truthfulness.
Naming is discretionary, and reputation for immorality is not a permitted impeachment trait.
Once a conviction is admitted under 609, at least the fact of conviction comes in.
pre: A defendant charged with cocaine distribution has a prior conviction for possession of cocaine for sale. The court excludes it from the government's case in chief under Rules 404(b) and 403. The defendant then testifies and denies the sale. The government offers the same conviction under Rule 609. Which statement is correct?

q: A defendant charged with sexual assault denies having any sexual contact with the complainant. A forensic examination found semen from an unidentified male, and DNA testing excluded the defendant. After complying with Rule 412(c), the defense makes four offers. Which has the strongest basis for admission?
o: Testimony that the complainant had intercourse with her boyfriend that afternoon, to explain the source of the semen.
Testimony that the complainant and the defendant had consensual sex twice the previous month, to prove she consented.
Testimony about the complainant's reputation for casual relationships, to show she was likely with someone else that day.
Her dating-app profile describing an interest in casual encounters, to show she was the kind of person who seeks them out.
oe: Correct. Rule 412(b)(1)(A) allows specific instances to show that someone other than the defendant was the source of semen, injury, or other physical evidence.
The defendant denies any contact, so consent isn't in issue. The with-the-accused exception serves a defense he isn't raising.
Reputation evidence is barred in criminal cases, and propensity reasoning is exactly what 412 forbids.
This is predisposition evidence, barred by 412(a).

q: Variation: The defendant now admits the intercourse and claims it was consensual. DNA confirms he is the source of the semen. Which offer now has the strongest basis for admission?
o: The two earlier consensual encounters between the complainant and the defendant, offered to prove consent.
Testimony that she had intercourse with her boyfriend that afternoon, to explain the source of the semen.
Testimony that she had several other partners that month, to show she was open to sex with new acquaintances.
Testimony that she dresses provocatively at parties, to show that she welcomed sexual attention that night.
oe: Correct. Rule 412(b)(1)(B) allows behavior with the accused, offered by the defendant, to prove consent.
The source is no longer disputed, so the source exception does no work.
Behavior with others offered to show consent is the classic forbidden inference.
This is predisposition evidence, barred by 412(a).
pre: A defendant charged with sexual assault denies having any sexual contact with the complainant. A forensic examination found semen from an unidentified male, and DNA testing excluded the defendant. After complying with Rule 412(c), the defense makes four offers. Which has the strongest basis for admission?

q: A defendant charged with rape claims the encounter was consensual. The defense makes four offers, each timely and procedurally proper. Which has the strongest claim to admission under Rule 412(b)(1)(C)?
o: The complainant was living with another man who saw her leave the defendant's car, giving her a motive to claim rape.
During the encounter she mentioned enjoying a similar act with a former partner, which the defendant says is needed for his story.
The defendant had heard rumors of her sexual history and therefore believed that she would consent that night.
She had consensual sex with several men she met at the same bar, which the defendant says shows she consents to strangers.
oe: Correct. Cross-examination showing a motive to fabricate is protected by the Confrontation Clause (Olden v. Kentucky).
Narrative integrity alone generally doesn't override the shield (Stephens v. Miller).
Belief in consent based on her reputation is usually excluded (Knox). Galvin's 404(b)-style proposal might treat it differently.
This is the propensity inference that 412(a) bars and that even Galvin's proposal would bar.

q: In a sexual-assault trial, the defense wants to cross-examine the complainant about earlier accusations. Which proposed inquiry falls outside Rule 412 altogether?
o: An accusation of rape against a classmate that she later admitted in a signed statement she had made up.
An accusation against a coworker that did not lead to charges, with nothing indicating that the accusation was false.
An accusation against a neighbor that resulted in his conviction, offered to show that she has been sexually active.
An accusation against an ex-boyfriend that she withdrew after they reconciled, offered to suggest that it was true.
oe: Correct. A proven false accusation isn't 'sexual behavior.' It's governed by 403, 404, and 608 (State v. Smith; Alvey, Problem 5.5).
Without proof of falsity, the inquiry implies other sexual activity and stays within 412.
This is sexual-behavior evidence offered for a forbidden purpose.
Suggesting the earlier accusation was true is evidence of sexual behavior, so 412 governs.

q: A defendant charged with assault arising from a bondage encounter on a first date claims the complainant consented. Before trial and after a proper 412(c) motion, he offers several emails. Which has the strongest basis for admission?
o: Her emails to him two days earlier describing her interest in bondage and suggesting they try it together.
Her emails to a friend a year earlier describing a bondage relationship with a former boyfriend.
Her emails to a dating site describing her sexual preferences, which the defendant never saw.
Emails from her former partner describing their bondage relationship, offered to show she enjoys rough sex.
oe: Correct. Her own communications to the defendant just before the encounter bear directly on consent and his understanding. The appellate court in Jovanovic (Problem 5.3) found excluding such emails was error.
This is behavior with others, offered to show predisposition. It's barred by 412(a).
This is predisposition evidence that the defendant never saw, so it can't bear on his understanding.
The forbidden inference, offered through someone else's account.
topic: Rape shield (412) — Communications with the accused

q: An employee sues her former employer for sexual harassment by her supervisor. Before trial, the employer files a sealed motion to introduce evidence that she had a consensual relationship with a different coworker, arguing that she could not have found the workplace's sexual atmosphere unwelcome. She has not offered evidence of her own reputation. Which standard governs?
o: It comes in only if its probative value substantially outweighs harm to her and unfair prejudice to any party.
Ordinary Rule 403 balancing applies, because Rule 412's protections are limited to complainants in criminal prosecutions.
The evidence is admissible, because by suing for harassment she placed her sexual conduct in controversy.
The evidence is inadmissible under any standard, because Rule 412 contains no exceptions in civil cases.
oe: Correct. Rule 412(b)(2) is a reverse-403 test favoring exclusion. Reputation evidence would also require that she put it in controversy (Jones v. Clinton, Problem 5.9).
Rule 412 applies in civil and criminal cases.
Suing doesn't waive the shield. Only reputation evidence turns on whether she placed it in controversy.
Rule 412(b)(2) supplies the civil exception through its balancing test.

q: On the first morning of a rape trial, defense counsel tells the judge for the first time that she plans to ask the complainant about a specific earlier partner under 412(b)(1)(A). She has filed nothing. Which response best reflects Rule 412?
o: Deny it absent good cause, because 412(c) requires a written motion and sealed hearing.
Permit the questions, because the source-of-semen exception applies automatically once the defense identifies a partner.
Permit the questions after excusing the jury briefly, because a short sidebar satisfies the rule's hearing requirement.
Permit the questions if the complainant consents, because the rule's procedures protect only her privacy interests.
oe: Correct. Rule 412(c) requires a written motion filed at least 14 days before trial unless the court sets another time for good cause, plus notice to the victim and a closed hearing.
The exceptions still have to go through the 412(c) procedure.
The rule requires a written motion, notice to the victim, and a sealed in camera hearing, not a sidebar.
The procedures also protect the court's process. Consent doesn't replace them.
